label: Y-incision
explanation: The autopsy internal exam classically begins with a Y-shaped incision extending from each shoulder to the mid-chest and down the midline, allowing the thoracic and abdominal cavities to be opened as shown.

label: Heart
explanation: The labeled superior/inferior vena cava, aorta, pulmonary artery and veins, atria, and ventricles identify this as a dissection of the heart, demonstrating the four-chamber cardiac anatomy.

label: Cirrhotic liver
explanation: The uniform micro/macronodular architecture with intervening fibrous bands in a liver from a chronic alcohol user is characteristic of cirrhosis, the end-stage of diffuse hepatic fibrosis and regenerative nodule formation.

label: Transfusion medicine
explanation: The instruments pictured are automated blood-bank analyzers used for ABO/Rh typing, antibody screening, and crossmatching to support safe blood transfusion.

label: Clinical chemistry
explanation: This is a clinical chemistry laboratory, which uses large automated chemistry analyzers to measure electrolytes, glucose, liver and kidney panels, and other biochemical analytes at high volume.

label: Microbiology
explanation: This is the microbiology laboratory, which cultures specimens on media plates to isolate and identify micro-organisms and guide antimicrobial therapy.

label: Disk diffusion test
explanation: This is a disk-diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) susceptibility test. A zone of inhibited growth around a disk means the antibiotic diffusing from it suppresses the organism, indicating susceptibility; absence of a zone indicates resistance.

label: Urinalysis
explanation: This is a urine dipstick being read against a color chart, part of the urinalysis chemical exam that assesses pH, protein, glucose, ketones, bilirubin, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, and blood.

label: HLA complex
explanation: The diagram shows the HLA (MHC) gene complex at 6p21. These genes encode cell-surface MHC molecules that present peptide antigens, allowing the immune system to distinguish self from non-self, which is the basis of transplant matching and rejection.

label: Fatty liver
explanation: The pale, yellowed, enlarged appearance is characteristic of hepatic steatosis, in which triglyceride accumulates in hepatocytes. Significant macrovesicular steatosis is a relative or absolute contraindication to using the liver for transplant.

label: Macrovesicular steatosis
explanation: A single large fat droplet pushing the nucleus to the edge of the hepatocyte defines macrovesicular steatosis. Confirmation of greater than 30 percent macrovesicular steatosis is associated with poor early graft function.

label: Bridging fibrosis
explanation: The trichrome stain colors collagen blue, revealing bridging fibrosis. Fibrosis is graded by extent of involvement and is an important determinant of donor organ viability.

label: Hepatocyte necrosis
explanation: Loss of nuclear staining with preserved cell outline is coagulative necrosis of hepatocytes. Greater than 10 percent necrosis may disqualify a donor organ from transplantation.

label: Interstitial fibrosis
explanation: Widening of the interstitium by collagen (fibrosis) accompanied by inflammatory cells constitutes interstitial fibrosis and inflammation, a key pathology assessed in donor kidney biopsies.

label: Arterial sclerosis
explanation: Arterial sclerosis in the kidney reflects deposition of collagenous matrix and smooth muscle between the endothelium and internal elastic lamina, thickening the intima and narrowing the lumen.

label: Arteriolar hyalinization
explanation: Deposition of homogeneous eosinophilic protein material in the arteriolar wall is arteriolar hyalinization (hyaline arteriolosclerosis), commonly associated with hypertension and diabetes in donor kidneys.

label: Glomerulosclerosis
explanation: Global glomerulosclerosis is scarring and hyalinization affecting more than half of the glomerulus, obliterating the capillary loops with acellular hyaline material. The proportion of sclerosed glomeruli helps determine kidney viability.

label: Hyperacute rejection
explanation: Preformed recipient antibodies against ABO or MHC antigens on graft endothelium activate complement within minutes to hours, causing thrombosis, ischemia, and necrosis (a type II hypersensitivity reaction). The glomerular fibrin thrombi shown are the histologic hallmark of hyperacute rejection.

label: Florid duct lesion
explanation: The florid duct lesion, a granulomatous destruction of interlobular bile ducts with surrounding lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, is the hallmark histologic finding of primary biliary cholangitis.

label: Primary sclerosing cholangitis
explanation: Concentric 'onion-skin' periductal fibrosis progressing to obliteration of the bile duct is the characteristic histology of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

label: Biliary beading
explanation: Multifocal strictures with intervening dilation ('beading') of the intra- and extrahepatic ducts on MRCP/ERCP is the gold-standard imaging finding of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

label: Chronic viral hepatitis
explanation: Hepatitis C rarely causes symptomatic acute infection but frequently becomes chronic, marked by portal lymphocytic/lymphoplasmacytic inflammation that can progress to cirrhosis.

label: Bridging fibrosis
explanation: The trichrome stain colors collagen blue, highlighting the delicate bridging fibrosis that develops later in the course of chronic hepatitis C.

label: Chondrosarcoma
explanation: This is a de-differentiated chondrosarcoma; despite anaplasia, the retained cartilage-like component identifies chondrocytes as the cell of origin.

label: Cellular adaptations
explanation: Metaplasia and the other reversible adaptations shown occur as protective responses to repeated or chronic cellular stress; if the stressor is removed, the cells can revert to their original type.

label: Barrett esophagus
explanation: Chronic acid reflux damages esophageal squamous epithelium, which is replaced by protective columnar epithelium with goblet cells; this glandular metaplasia defines Barrett esophagus and carries a risk of adenocarcinoma.

label: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
explanation: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma forms infiltrative duct-like glandular structures composed of neoplastic cells, commonly harbors KRAS mutations, and carries a very poor prognosis.

label: Melanoma
explanation: Cutaneous melanoma arises from transformed melanocytes, which produce brown melanin pigment visible histologically; activating BRAF (V600E) mutations are a common oncogenic driver and therapeutic target.

label: Chronic myeloid leukemia
explanation: CML marrow is hypercellular with granulocytic hyperplasia, eosinophilia, and small hypolobated megakaryocytes; it is driven by the BCR::ABL fusion producing constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.

label: Rosettes
explanation: Homer Wright rosettes (radial cells around a fibrillar center) and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (cells around a true lumen) are both characteristic histologic features of retinoblastoma.

label: Neurofibromatosis 1
explanation: Café-au-lait macules and multiple cutaneous neurofibromas are hallmark manifestations of neurofibromatosis type 1, caused by loss of the NF1 GTPase-activating protein on chromosome 17.

label: Hallmarks of cancer
explanation: The figure depicts the eight fundamental hallmarks of cancer—the capabilities neoplasms acquire to sustain growth, evade suppression and immune destruction, and invade and metastasize.

label: Mitotic figures
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: The arrows point to mitotic figures (condensed dividing chromosomes staining dark purple). Abundant mitoses are a morphologic marker of rapid cellular proliferation, seen here in a medulloblastoma.

label: Cellular swelling
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: Depleted ATP impairs Na+/K+ pumps, causing water influx and cellular swelling with pale, eosinophilic cytoplasm. This is a hallmark of reversible injury and resolves if the stimulus is removed.

label: Mitochondria
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: Mitochondrial damage lowers ATP (impairing energy-dependent functions) and raises ROS production, which together damage lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Failure to reverse mitochondrial dysfunction marks irreversible injury.

label: Karyolysis
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: Karyolysis is the fading of basophilic nuclear staining as chromatin is degraded. It is distinct from pyknosis (shrunken dark nuclei) and karyorrhexis (nuclear fragmentation), accompanying the eosinophilia and swelling of injured cells.

label: Bilirubin
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: Bilirubin is a yellow-brown pigment from heme breakdown that accumulates when bile excretion is impaired. It is distinct from hemosiderin, the iron-containing blood breakdown product.

label: Dystrophic calcification
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: Dystrophic calcification is calcium deposition in damaged or dying tissue under normal systemic calcium homeostasis, as in this atherosclerotic aortic valve. Metastatic calcification instead occurs in normal tissue with hypercalcemia.

label: Endometrial hyperplasia
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: Excess estrogen drives increased proliferation of endometrial glandular cells (hyperplasia), producing a bulky lining and a cause of abnormal uterine bleeding.

label: Cell injury
brick: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation
explanation: The figure summarizes how decreased ATP, increased cytosolic calcium, reactive oxygen species, and membrane/DNA damage act through multiple downstream effects to cause cell injury.

label: Xeroderma pigmentosum
explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from loss-of-function mutations in nucleotide excision repair, leaving patients unable to remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, producing severe photosensitivity, freckling in sun-exposed areas, and greatly increased skin cancer risk.

label: Mismatch repair
explanation: The figure depicts mismatch repair. Germline mutation of a mismatch-repair gene (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) causes Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer), producing microsatellite instability and markedly increased colorectal and endometrial cancer risk.

label: MMR immunohistochemistry
explanation: Loss of nuclear staining for MLH1 and PMS2 (which form a heterodimer, so loss of MLH1 destabilizes PMS2) with preserved MSH2/MSH6 indicates a mismatch-repair-deficient tumor. Such deficiency underlies microsatellite instability and is characteristic of Lynch-syndrome-associated cancers.

label: Ataxia telangiectasia
explanation: The dilated vessels (telangiectasia) with early-onset ataxia indicate ataxia telangiectasia, caused by defective nonhomologous end joining of double-strand breaks. The same defect impairs V(D)J recombination, producing immunodeficiency, and predisposes to leukemia and lymphoma.

label: Small cell carcinoma
explanation: The morphology (small blue cells, scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, dispersed chromatin) is that of small cell lung carcinoma, a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine tumor derived from Kulchitsky cells. This origin explains its capacity for ectopic hormone production (ACTH, ADH) and neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes.

label: Pap smear
explanation: The enlarged, hyperchromatic cells with increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio represent a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). This precancerous dysplasia of the cervix is caused by persistent infection with high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV), which is why HPV testing has become a key screening tool alongside the Pap smear.

label: Colon adenoma
explanation: The images show colonic adenomas (adenomatous polyps). Through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, crowded neoplastic glands progressively accumulate mutations and can invade beyond the basement membrane into the lamina propria, giving rise to colorectal adenocarcinoma. Screening colonoscopy allows their removal before malignant transformation.

label: Mammography
explanation: The mammogram shows clustered microcalcifications, a classic early sign of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Biopsy reveals neoplastic cells expanding a duct without invasion past the basement membrane, along with the characteristic chunky intraductal calcifications. Detecting DCIS by mammography allows treatment before progression to invasive disease.

label: Mediastinal lymphadenopathy
explanation: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma classically presents with painless enlarged supradiaphragmatic (neck and mediastinal) lymphadenopathy, seen here as bulky anterior mediastinal and paratracheal adenopathy on CT.

label: Reed-Sternberg cell
explanation: The bilobed, owl-eye Reed-Sternberg cell with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli is the pathognomonic histologic finding of classic Hodgkin lymphoma, roughly half of which are EBV-associated.

label: Burkitt lymphoma
explanation: The pale tingible body macrophages scattered among the dark neoplastic B-cells create the 'starry sky' appearance characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma.

label: Jaw mass
explanation: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma is virtually always EBV-positive and classically presents in African children as a large, rapidly growing mandibular/jaw mass.

label: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
explanation: The EBV-associated non-keratinizing (undifferentiated) subtype of nasopharyngeal carcinoma shows undifferentiated epithelial cells with a dense lymphocytic infiltrate.

label: Hepatocellular carcinoma
explanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma most often arises from longstanding inflammation-mediated cellular damage and cirrhosis; hepatitis B virus is the leading worldwide cause.

label: Verruca vulgaris
explanation: Verruca vulgaris (common warts) are benign hyperkeratotic squamous papillomas caused by low-risk HPV serotypes 1, 2, 4, and 7.

label: Flower cell
explanation: A multi-lobulated, flower-shaped nucleus is seen in the acute phase of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma associated with HTLV-1 infection.

label: Gastric adenocarcinoma
explanation: Chronic H. pylori infection drives the stepwise cascade to gastric adenocarcinoma; endoscopic screening in high-incidence regions detects early, resectable lesions.

label: Chronic gastritis
explanation: H. pylori induces chronic gastritis characterized by a mucosal infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells, the first step in the cascade toward adenocarcinoma.

label: Intestinal metaplasia
explanation: Intestinal metaplasia (goblet and Paneth cells replacing gastric epithelium) is a premalignant step in the H. pylori-driven progression toward gastric adenocarcinoma.

label: Gastric adenocarcinoma
explanation: High-grade dysplasia becomes invasive gastric adenocarcinoma when the neoplastic cells invade through the basement membrane into surrounding tissues.

label: MALT lymphoma
explanation: Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the stomach is associated with H. pylori and shows an increased population of small neoplastic B-cells; many cases regress after eradication.

label: Schistosoma eggs
explanation: Schistosoma haematobium eggs (terminal spine) cause chronic bladder inflammation and metaplasia, predisposing to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

label: Cell injury
explanation: The diagram shows a continuum: mild, short-lived injury permits adaptation or reversible injury, whereas severe, prolonged injury exceeds the cell's capacity to recover and drives it to death by necrosis or apoptosis. Thus the intensity and duration of the stimulus is the key determinant.

label: Cell injury mechanisms
explanation: ATP is required to run the Na+/K+ ATPase; when ATP falls, the pump fails, sodium and water accumulate intracellularly, and the cell swells. The other mechanisms shown (calcium influx, ROS, membrane damage, DNA damage) act through separate routes.

label: BCL2
explanation: BCL2 keeps the outer mitochondrial membrane impermeable, blocking cytochrome c release and preventing apoptosis. The t(14;18) translocation places BCL2 under an immunoglobulin promoter, causing overexpression that resists apoptosis and produces follicular lymphoma.

label: Apoptotic cell
explanation: Apoptotic cells shrink, become densely eosinophilic, and show condensed nuclei; because apoptosis is controlled and cells are cleared by phagocytes, there is little or no inflammation. Necrosis, by contrast, spills cell contents and provokes a prominent inflammatory response.

label: Coagulative necrosis
explanation: Coagulative necrosis preserves the tissue architecture (ghost outlines) while cells die, and is the hallmark of ischemic infarction in solid organs other than the brain. The wedge-shaped pale infarct and retained cell outlines are classic.

label: Liquefactive necrosis
explanation: Liquefactive necrosis results when hydrolytic enzymes digest dead tissue into a viscous liquid. It is the characteristic pattern of central nervous system infarcts and of abscesses. Protein denaturation instead yields coagulative necrosis.

label: Gangrenous necrosis
explanation: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term for necrosis of a limb or digits, typically from loss of blood supply. Dry gangrene is largely coagulative; wet gangrene adds superimposed liquefactive necrosis from bacterial infection.

label: Caseous necrosis
explanation: Caseous necrosis has a friable, cheese-like gross appearance and is classically caused by tuberculosis. Microscopically it shows granulomas with fragmented, granular debris, distinguishing it from other necrosis patterns.

label: Fat necrosis
explanation: In fat necrosis, released lipases (e.g., in acute pancreatitis) break down adipose tissue; the liberated free fatty acids combine with calcium in a saponification reaction to form the chalky-white deposits seen here.

label: Fibrinoid necrosis
explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis occurs when immune complexes and plasma proteins (fibrin) deposit in vessel walls, producing a bright pink, smudgy appearance with inflammation. It is characteristic of autoimmune small-vessel vasculitides.

label: Punch biopsy
explanation: A punch biopsy uses a cylindrical blade rotated into the skin to remove a full-thickness core of tissue for histologic evaluation.

label: Excisional biopsy
explanation: An excisional biopsy removes the entire lesion plus a surrounding safety margin of normal-appearing skin, making it both diagnostic and potentially curative.

label: FFPE blocks
explanation: Surgical specimens are typically processed as formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) blocks; formalin cross-links proteins to preserve tissue morphology for at least 10 years.

label: H&E stain
explanation: In H&E staining, eosin stains cytoplasmic and extracellular components pink while hematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple.

label: GMS stain
explanation: The Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain deposits silver on fungal cell walls, making fungal hyphae and yeast readily visible.

label: Immunohistochemistry
explanation: Immunohistochemistry uses antibodies against a specific antigen, and a chromogen produces brown color where the antigen is present. Cytokeratin positivity here helps identify the neoplasm as a carcinoma.

label: Papillary thyroid carcinoma
explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is characterized by nuclear enlargement, nuclear overlap, and optically clear (Orphan Annie eye) nuclei with grooves.

label: Pap smear
explanation: A high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear enlargement, and irregular nuclear membranes are worrisome cytologic features, contrasting with the abundant cytoplasm of the normal intermediate squamous cell.

label: Pneumonia
explanation: The opaque areas correspond to alveolar spaces filled with purulent exudate, a pattern consistent with bacterial pneumonia.

label: Serous inflammation
explanation: A blister formed by accumulation of protein-poor, cell-poor (transudate-like) fluid separating the epidermis represents serous inflammation.

label: Fibrinous pericarditis
explanation: Increased vascular permeability allows fibrinogen to leak and deposit as fibrin on the pericardial surface, producing a fibrinous exudate (fibrinous pericarditis).

label: Duodenal ulcer
explanation: An ulcer is a local defect of an epithelial surface produced by sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue, here a chronic duodenal ulcer.

label: Lymphocyte
explanation: A small cell dominated by a round nucleus with scant cytoplasm is a lymphocyte. Neutrophils have multilobed nuclei, eosinophils have bilobed nuclei with red granules, monocytes are larger with reniform nuclei, and basophils contain dark blue granules.

label: Tuberculous granuloma
explanation: Caseating (necrotizing) granulomas in the lung are the hallmark of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. The listed pyogenic bacteria produce acute suppurative inflammation with abscesses rather than organized granulomas with central caseous necrosis.

label: Non-necrotizing granuloma
explanation: Compact, non-caseating granulomas that lack central necrosis are classic for sarcoidosis. Tuberculosis and histoplasmosis usually caseate, cat-scratch disease shows suppurative granulomas, and while Crohn's granulomas are non-caseating they occur in the gut, not the lung.

label: Sarcoid granuloma
explanation: Sarcoid granulomas are non-caseating, so they lack the central caseous necrosis typical of tuberculosis. They still contain multinucleated giant cells, epithelioid macrophages, lymphocytes, and a surrounding fibrous rim, so those are present rather than absent.

label: Extracellular matrix
explanation: The layer shown between epithelium and interstitium is the basement membrane, a specialized extracellular matrix rich in type IV collagen and laminin that provides an anchoring, supporting surface for the growth of epithelial, endothelial, and smooth muscle cells.

label: Second intention
explanation: Healing by secondary intention occurs with extensive tissue loss: the large defect fills with granulation tissue, and myofibroblasts form a contractile network that pulls the wound together, reducing the defect over weeks.

label: Keloid scar
explanation: A keloid is exuberant scarring that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound and shows thick, brightly eosinophilic collagen arranged haphazardly; unlike hypertrophic scars, which stay within the original wound and may regress, keloids do not regress on their own.

label: Chronic wounds
explanation: An ulcer is a wound lacking an intact epithelial surface; histologically it correlates with loss of the overlying epithelium plus surface necrotic debris, inflammation, and underlying granulation tissue, as seen in these venous, arterial, diabetic, and pressure-related chronic wounds.

label: Neurons
brick: Introduction to Histology and Histology of Connective Tissue
explanation: Typical neurons have elongated processes (dendrites and axons) and a cell body with a single nucleus and a prominent nucleolus. Their appearance varies somewhat by brain location. Nervous tissue is made of two cell types: neurons and glial cells.

label: Peripheral nerve
brick: Introduction to Histology and Histology of Connective Tissue
explanation: In a longitudinal section of normal peripheral nerve, the nerve fibers look wavy, and the dark nuclei belong to Schwann cells. Oligodendrocytes do the equivalent myelinating job only in the CNS.

label: Adipose tissue
brick: Introduction to Histology and Histology of Connective Tissue
explanation: Adipocytes are resident connective tissue cells that store, make and release fat. In H&E preparations the fat washes out, leaving only a round white space with a nucleus pushed to the edge. This is mature adipose tissue.

label: Fibroblast
brick: Introduction to Histology and Histology of Connective Tissue
explanation: Fibroblasts make collagen and elastic fibers and much of the ground substance. Resting fibroblasts have an oval nucleus; active ones become fusiform, with abundant RER and Golgi. They normally do not divide by mitosis except during wound healing.

label: Cardiac muscle
brick: Histology of Muscle and Nervous Tissue
explanation: The cells are striated (S) with centrally placed nuclei (N) and dark transverse lines (I), the intercalated discs. Intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle. Skeletal muscle has many peripheral nuclei and no intercalated discs, and smooth muscle is not striated.

label: Neuron
brick: Histology of Muscle and Nervous Tissue
explanation: Myelin, a mixture of phospholipids and proteins, insulates the axon and increases the speed of nerve impulse conduction. Dendrites receive stimuli, microglia scavenge debris, ependymal cells handle CSF, and endothelial cells with astrocytes form the blood-brain barrier.

label: Neuron
brick: Histology of Muscle and Nervous Tissue
explanation: The neuron cell body has a single nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. Its cytoplasm contains abundant rough ER that stains deep purple and granular, called Nissl substance. The axon hillock is pale because it lacks Nissl substance.

label: Ependymal cells
brick: Histology of Muscle and Nervous Tissue
explanation: Ependymal cells are columnar or cuboidal epithelial cells that line the brain's ventricles and the central canal of the spinal cord. In some areas they have cilia that help move CSF, and modified ependymal cells help form the choroid plexus, which produces CSF.

label: Oligodendrocyte
brick: Histology of Muscle and Nervous Tissue
explanation: Oligodendrocytes send out processes that myelinate multiple CNS axons. In multiple sclerosis, autoimmune demyelination of CNS axons in the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves impairs conduction, causing optic neuritis, incoordination, numbness and tingling, and fatigue.

label: Schwann cell
brick: Histology of Muscle and Nervous Tissue
explanation: Schwann cells myelinate axons in the PNS. As each cell wraps an axon, its cytoplasm is squeezed out, forming the major dense line and the intraperiod line. Unlike oligodendrocytes, which can myelinate multiple axons, each Schwann cell myelinates only one segment of one axon.

label: Peripheral nerve
brick: Histology of Muscle and Nervous Tissue
explanation: On light microscopy, peripheral nerve is a wavy, pink-textured bundle surrounded by perineurium. Axons appear as dark-pink lines with bubbly-looking myelin around them, and you can see the oval nuclei of Schwann cells and the flatter nuclei of fibroblasts.

label: Goblet cell
explanation: These are goblet cells, which are unicellular exocrine glands named for their wine-glass shape. They are scattered among the columnar cells lining the intestinal and respiratory tracts and release their product (mucus) by exocytosis. Their mucin-filled cytoplasm looks pale on H&E.

label: Sebaceous gland
explanation: S marks sebaceous glands, which sit beside hair follicles and are the classic holocrine glands. Their cells accumulate lipid-rich sebum until the whole cell breaks apart and becomes the secretion. This is also why a sebaceous cyst comes back after simple drainage: the glandular lining stays behind.

label: Gap junction
explanation: This is a gap junction. Connexins assemble into a cylindrical connexon that can open or close, which lets small ions and molecules pass directly from one cell to the next. That allows epithelial cells, and cardiac muscle cells, to act as a coordinated unit. The distractors describe the other junctions: tight junctions seal the space, hemidesmosomes anchor to the basement membrane, belt desmosomes link actin, and spot desmosomes link intermediate filaments.

label: Abscess
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: An abscess is a localized collection of purulence (liquefactive necrosis of dead and dying neutrophils and debris) with a surrounding wall of connective tissue that attempts to wall off the infection. It is the classic lesion of suppurative inflammation caused by pyogenic bacteria such as staphylococci.

label: Treponema pallidum
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: The spiral (corkscrew) morphology seen black on silver stain is characteristic of the spirochete Treponema pallidum, the cause of syphilis. Primary and secondary syphilis produce perivascular lymphoplasmacytic inflammation; tertiary syphilis becomes granulomatous (gummas).

label: Foreign body granuloma
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: Granulomas can form in response to foreign material. Here a splinter, seen in cross-section as a white oval object, is surrounded by a granulomatous reaction of macrophages and giant cells - a foreign body granuloma, not an infectious one.

label: Malar rash
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: A butterfly-shaped malar rash with arthritis, oral ulcers and pancytopenia indicates systemic lupus erythematosus. ANA plus anti-dsDNA or anti-Smith antibodies are present in SLE. PR3-ANCA = GPA, anti-collagen IV = Goodpasture, SS-A/SS-B = Sjogren, elevated ACE = sarcoidosis.

label: Purpura
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is a childhood syndrome (ages 3-8) of purpuric skin lesions on extensor surfaces and buttocks, abdominal pain/GI bleeding, arthralgias and renal abnormalities. Like SLE, it is due to immune complex deposition, usually IgA +/- IgG and C3.

label: Asteroid body
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: Asteroid bodies - a star resembling structure in a cleared circle within histiocytes - may be seen in the non-necrotizing granulomas of sarcoidosis. They are not specific, and sarcoidosis remains a diagnosis of exclusion (infections must be ruled out).

label: Erythema nodosum
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: Erythema nodosum refers to red, tender nodules most commonly on the anterior and lateral lower extremities. It is a non-specific finding but is one of the cutaneous manifestations of sarcoidosis.

label: Lupus pernio
brick: Pathologic Manifestations of Infectious and Immune-related Diseases
explanation: Lupus pernio - painful lesions of the nose, beneath the eyes and cheeks - is a cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis (along with erythema nodosum and maculopapular lesions). Despite its name, it is not the malar rash of SLE.

label: Omentum
brick: Cancer Growth, Metastasis, and Medications Overview
explanation: Seeding requires an open space such as the peritoneal cavity, pleural cavity, subarachnoid space, or joint cavities. Ovarian carcinoma is the classic example, seeding the peritoneal cavity and omentum.
